title: The competitive response framework for case interviews
description: "How should the client respond to a rival's move?" A rival cuts prices, launches a product or enters the market. The structure, the first question to ask, and
hook: When a rival cuts prices or launches something new, clients often want to react immediately. Your job in the case is to slow down and ask what is really at stake. Here is a calm way to structure a competitive response question.
body:
When you will use it

A rival cuts prices, launches a product or enters the market.

This is a decide question: "Should we do this?" Test it against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

What exactly did they do, and which of our customers does it touch?

One good question at the start can halve the work. It tells you where to look, and it shows the interviewer you are thinking about the client, not reciting a list.

The structure

  • How exposed are we?
    • Customers at risk
    • Revenue and margin at risk
  • Why are they doing it? (can they keep it up?)
    • Which segments they want
    • Their economics
  • Our options
    • Do nothing
    • Defend our customers (loyalty · contracts · promotions)
    • Match them (adjust price · upgrade product)
    • Copy their offer
    • Partner or buy

Say it out loud as a short sentence per branch, then say which branch you would look at first and why. That last part, your hypothesis, is what most candidates forget.

Make it your own

Size the threat before choosing a response, and compare every option with doing nothing. Doing nothing is right when little profit is at risk.

Interviewers can tell when a structure has been memorised. Swap the general words for words about this client: not "costs", but "fuel and crew costs" for an airline.

Practise with real prompts

Read each prompt, take two minutes to sketch your own structure, then compare.

1. A rival has cut prices 20% on our best-selling product. How do we respond?

Show a model structure
  • The threat: What exactly did they cut, where, for how long?; Their costs: can they sustain it?
  • Impact on us: Customers lost so far and at risk; Profit at risk under each scenario
  • Our options: Match, partly match, hold, differentiate; Target only the customers at risk
  • Their likely reaction: Price war risk; How long they can keep it up vs us

Where to start: Impact first: how many customers actually switch before we react.

The trap: Matching the price immediately without sizing what is really at risk.

2. How should an electricity company respond to the growth of rooftop solar?

Show a model structure
  • Impact: Lost demand and revenue; Grid still needed at night and in winter
  • Defend: Pricing: fixed charges vs per kWh; Regulation and grid fees
  • New services: Selling and installing solar and batteries; EV charging, home energy management
  • Costs: Grid and plant costs as demand falls; Closing or selling unneeded plants

Where to start: Impact: how much revenue is at risk and how fast.

The trap: Only fighting solar through tariffs and regulation instead of also selling it.

3. A shampoo brand has lost 4 points of market share in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Where share went: To which rivals or own-label; Which channels and stores
  • Price: Our price gap vs rivals; Promotions frequency
  • Product and brand: New launches by rivals; Advertising and awareness
  • Distribution: Shelf space, out of stocks; Online visibility

Where to start: Where the share went: losing to own-label is a price problem, to a rival launch a product problem.

The trap: Spending more on advertising before knowing who took the share.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. You can see this tree drawn step by step, and every other core framework, on the free frameworks page.
